profile.reading:
This is a Carfax facility in Boone County, Missouri, in Columbia's Lemone Industrial Park, the area where Carfax itself was founded in 1984 by Ewin Barnett III and Robert Daniel Clark. The company's original product, a vehicle history report distributed to auto dealers by fax starting in 1986, is the source of its name, and Columbia has remained a significant operational base for the company through several changes of corporate ownership since.

Carfax was acquired by R.L. Polk and Company in 1999, then became part of IHS in 2013, IHS Markit in 2016, and S&P Global following that company's 2022 merger with IHS Markit. Carfax now describes itself on its own site as part of Mobility Global, reflecting a subsequent restructuring of S&P Global's automotive and mobility data businesses into their own operation. Through all of these changes, Carfax has continued to describe itself as the expert in vehicle history since 1984, tying its identity directly back to its Missouri origins.

Carfax's core product is a vehicle history report built from a database the company describes as containing more than 35 billion records drawn from over 151,000 sources, including motor vehicle departments across all 50 US states and 10 Canadian provinces, along with auction houses, insurance companies, repair shops, and law enforcement agencies. Matching and reporting against that volume of data requires substantial backend technology infrastructure, and Columbia has long served as a hub for Carfax's technical and data operations alongside its corporate offices elsewhere.

No specific power capacity, technical square footage, or facility-level construction date for this Columbia building could be confirmed, and none are estimated here. What can be said with confidence is that this address sits inside the industrial park associated with Carfax's founding city, consistent with a technology and operations campus tied to the company's origins rather than a retail storefront or an unrelated business carrying the same name.

Beyond vehicle history reports, Carfax's current product lineup includes used and new car listings that pair every result with a free history report, a car care app that tracks recalls and service records for registered vehicles, and research tools covering specs, predicted reliability, and predicted resale value for most models sold since the 2000 model year. The company also licenses its data and reporting tools to auto dealers, service shops, insurers, and government agencies as business customers, alongside the consumer-facing report product that made its name. That breadth of products, spanning consumer web and mobile tools, dealer-facing services, and large-scale data licensing, is the kind of operation that benefits from keeping core data and engineering functions close to where the company got its start, which is the most likely explanation for why Columbia continues to carry weight in Carfax's operations more than four decades after its founding there.
